newsitem.title: USA: More U.S. wireless firms seek FCC help on payments.
newsitem.headline: More U.S. wireless firms seek FCC help on payments.

text.p: More communications firms are asking Uncle Sam for help to pay for licenses, complicating government efforts to help struggling companies pay for $10.2 billion in wireless phone rights won at auction.

Three firms have told the Federal Communications Commission in documents filed with the agency that they are looking for equal treatment if the agency makes payment easier for the nearly 90 firms that bid at a pricey wireless phone auction held last year by the FCC.

Two of the three think any easier payment terms should be extended to others -- possibly dozens and dozens of firms that offer a variety of services ranging from paging to wireless cable television that are transmitted over the airwaves.
Industry and government officials said the small companies could take legal action if the FCC rejects the request.

The firms won licenses at FCC auctions for advanced messaging, dispatch and paging services. They argue that special treatment for the phone firms would hurt their own businesses, because they compete with wireless telephony.

"They're competing for the same capital. They're competing for the same customers," said attorney Terry Romine of Lukas McGowan Nace & Gutierrez, which represents CONXUS Communications Inc. CONXUS won five licenses in 1994 to create a nationwide two-way messaging system.

The other two companies are Morris Communications Inc. and Creative Airtime Services. Both won licenses at a 1996 auction to offer specialized mobile services such as dispatch, paging, phone and messaging.
Creative Airtime believes equal terms should be extended to any FCC auction winner that is paying for its licenses in installment payments under a special program for small firms.

About 350 firms who have been in various airwave auctions are eligible for the installment program. They are on top of the 87 firms that bid $10.2 billion last year for the right to offer an advanced cellular service called "personal communications services," or PCS.

It's unclear whether the FCC ultimately will cobble together a rescue plan for the PCS companies struggling to make their payments for the licenses to the FCC. There is strong pressure within the agency to do little or nothing.
But the demand for equal treatment has not made the FCC's task any easier, FCC and government officials agreed.
"We're likely to be challenged if we do something for one (wireless service), but not other competitively situated services," said an FCC official.
Said a government official: "First, we've got to figure out whether we're going to do anything at all" for the PCS companies.
"Secondly, we've got to figure out whether the rationale for doing something in this case compels us to do something similar in other similar cases."
Many top PCS bidders, accounting for billions of dollars in bids, have since gotten into hot water and threatened to default unless the FCC develops some type of rescue plan.

FCC officials are studying whether to give the companies easier terms to repay the agency for the licenses -- such as converting quarterly interest payments to the FCC into annual payments, or deferring the payments for several years.
They also are mulling an amnesty program under which the companies could turn in their licenses for reauction.
The FCC ultimtely may decide to do nothing, a move that would raise the specter of a massive default and a legal fight for the FCC to get the licenses back, officials said.
